quote: Wie kann man eine Primzahlmaschine construiren, welche bei beständiger Heizung immer mehr Primzahlen liefert.
english: How can one construct a prime-number machine which, with continuous heating, delivers more and more primes?
topic: Notes on a hypothetical prime-number machine and the limits of what it can prove, a struck-out remark on successive osculating circles of a curve, deciding primality in finite time, and a remark praising Weierstrass as the Euclid of analysis.

triage.modern_statement: Is there a mechanical procedure (in modern terms, an algorithm or Turing/register machine) that, given unlimited time and energy, outputs an unbounded sequence of primes? Put another way: is the set of primes effectively enumerable, and can a fixed machine or formula produce it? Read literally, the answer is trivially yes, since trial division or the sieve of Eratosthenes decides primality in finite time. Given the page context about the limits of what such a machine can prove, Hilbert seems to be using the prime machine as an example of mechanical computation, not posing a hard open problem about primes.
triage.answered_by: The literal question was implicitly settled by classical algorithms (sieve, trial division); there is no specific later 'answerer.' Concrete machines and formulas were built later: D. H. Lehmer's mechanical sieve machines (bicycle-chain sieve with results published 1928, gear sieve 1932); Jones, Sato, Wada and Wiens (Amer. Math. Monthly 83, 1976), a polynomial whose positive values are exactly the primes, building on the Matiyasevich/MRDP theorem; and J. H. Conway's FRACTRAN program PRIMEGAME (1987), a literal 'prime-producing machine.' The idea of a 'machine' was made precise by Turing in 1936, but I did not source that here.

evidence.claim: Conway (1987) gave a FRACTRAN program called PRIMEGAME that finds successive primes. FRACTRAN can be seen as a kind of register machine.
Conway's 'prime-producing machine' is made of fractions: start with 2 and repeatedly multiply by the first fraction that gives an integer.
Jones, Sato, Wada and Wiens, 'Diophantine Representation of the Set of Prime Numbers', Amer. Math. Monthly 83(6), 1976, pp. 449-464.
D. H. Lehmer built mechanical sieve computers: a bicycle-chain sieve and, in 1932, a faster gear-driven sieve.
Lehmer published results from the bicycle-chain machine in 1928 and from the gear machine in 1933.

triage.why: As stated, the question asks only whether primes can be produced mechanically without end. That is elementary: the sieve and trial division do it, and the same page notes that primality can be decided in finite time. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Later work did produce explicit prime-generating machines and formulas (Lehmer's sieves, the 1976 JSWW polynomial, Conway's PRIMEGAME), which shows the idea was realized. However, none of these sources links Hilbert's note to that work. Hilbert's real interest, what such a machine can or cannot prove, points toward the decidability questions settled in the 1930s, but my sources do not tie this note to them, so I won't claim that link. Making primality testing efficient is still studied, but this note does not ask about efficiency.
